subChunks.title: GROUP_CONCAT, STRING_AGG, and Array Aggregation
subChunks.hookHtml: Sometimes you want to aggregate text values into a single comma-separated string — like showing all quest titles for each apprentice in one row. That is string aggregation.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
GROUP_CONCAT (SQLite / MySQL)

SELECT a.name,
       GROUP_CONCAT(q.title ORDER BY q.title SEPARATOR ', ') AS quests
FROM   apprentices AS a
JOIN   quest_completions AS qc ON qc.apprentice_id = a.id
JOIN   quests AS q ON q.id = qc.quest_id
GROUP BY a.name;

In SQLite, GROUP_CONCAT(col) uses comma by default and does not support ORDER BY inside the function — the overall ORDER BY controls sequence.

STRING_AGG (PostgreSQL)

SELECT a.name,
       STRING_AGG(q.title, ', ' ORDER BY q.title) AS quests
FROM   apprentices AS a
JOIN   quest_completions AS qc ON qc.apprentice_id = a.id
JOIN   quests AS q ON q.id = qc.quest_id
GROUP BY a.name;

ARRAY_AGG (PostgreSQL)

SELECT a.name, ARRAY_AGG(q.title ORDER BY q.title) AS quest_array
FROM   apprentices AS a
JOIN   quest_completions AS qc ON qc.apprentice_id = a.id
JOIN   quests AS q ON q.id = qc.quest_id
GROUP BY a.name;

Returns a PostgreSQL array rather than a delimited string. Useful for returning structured data to application code.

When to use it

String aggregation is useful for display purposes and reporting. Avoid storing aggregated strings in the database — they are hard to query. Keep data normalised; aggregate at query time.

storyBeats.text: The report format asks: one row per apprentice, all their quest titles in a single cell separated by commas.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: GROUP_CONCAT in SQLite, STRING_AGG in PostgreSQL. They collapse multiple rows into one delimited string per group. Use them for display and reporting — but never store the result back in the table. The moment you store a comma-separated string in a column, you have denormalised your schema and queries become painful.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
🪄 Quest list per apprentice

For each apprentice who has completed at least one quest, return their name and a comma-separated list of quest titles as completed_quests. Use GROUP_CONCAT.
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
SELECT a.name,
       GROUP_CONCAT(q.title) AS completed_quests
FROM   apprentices AS a
JOIN   quest_completions AS qc ON qc.apprentice_id = a.id
JOIN   quests AS q ON q.id = qc.quest_id
GROUP BY a.name
ORDER BY a.name;

guidedPracticeTests.label: Returns rows with name and completed_quests columns
guidedPracticeTests.setup: CREATE TABLE apprentices (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, rank TEXT NOT NULL, xp INTEGER NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE quests (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL, difficulty TEXT NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE quest_completions (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, apprentice_id INTEGER NOT NULL, quest_id INTEGER NOT NULL); INSERT INTO apprentices VALUES (1,'Alice','Apprentice',1200),(2,'Bjorn','Adept',2400),(3,'Cassia','Mage',4800); INSERT INTO quests VALUES (1,'Defeat the Shade','Hard'),(2,'Brew Mana Potion','Easy'),(3,'Decode Ancient Runes','Hard'); INSERT INTO quest_completions VALUES (1,2,1),(2,3,3),(3,1,2),(4,2,3);

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Return each mentor's name and a GROUP_CONCAT of their apprentices' names as students. Only include mentors who have at least 2 apprentices. Order by mentor name.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what GROUP_CONCAT does and why storing the aggregated result back in the database as a column is bad practice.

options: Aggregates multiple row values for a group into a single delimited string
Counts the number of non-NULL values in the group
Concatenates a column value with itself
Returns the first value in the group
questions.answer: Aggregates multiple row values for a group into a single delimited string
questions.explanation: GROUP_CONCAT is an aggregate function that collects multiple row values and combines them into one string, separated by a delimiter (comma by default in MySQL/SQLite).

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, which function is the equivalent of SQLite's GROUP_CONCAT?
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL uses STRING_AGG(expression, delimiter). It also supports an ORDER BY inside the function: STRING_AGG(col, ', ' ORDER BY col).

questions.prompt: GROUP_CONCAT with GROUP BY name and a JOIN will show quests for each apprentice. What happens to apprentices with no quest completions?
options: They are excluded — the INNER JOIN filters them out
They appear with NULL in the completed_quests column
They appear with an empty string
questions.answer: They are excluded — the INNER JOIN filters them out
questions.explanation: INNER JOIN excludes rows with no match. Apprentices with no quest completions have no rows in quest_completions, so they are filtered out. Use LEFT JOIN to include them with NULL.

questions.prompt: Why is storing `tags = 'fire,ice,water'` as a comma-delimited string in one column a poor database design?
options: It violates First Normal Form — you cannot query individual tags with WHERE, cannot index them, and cannot join them to other tables easily
It is only a problem if there are more than 10 tags
Comma-delimited strings prevent string aggregation functions from working
It uses more storage than an integer array
questions.answer: It violates First Normal Form — you cannot query individual tags with WHERE, cannot index them, and cannot join them to other tables easily
questions.explanation: Storing multiple values in a single column makes them hard to query, impossible to index individually, and awkward to join. The correct design is a separate tags table with one tag per row.
